evidence: src/application/PlaceOrderUseCase.ts: execute() delegates the stock decision to the domain via this.catalog.canReserve(item.productId, item.quantity) instead of computing it itself
src/application/PlaceOrderUseCase.ts: stock changes go through this.catalog.reserve(...), and the order is created with the domain factory createOrder(...)
src/application/PlaceOrderUseCase.ts: saving goes through the injected OrderRepository abstraction (this.orderRepository.save(order)); the file contains no database, HTTP or framework code
src/application/PlaceOrderUseCase.ts: inline ID generation (`order-${Date.now()}-...`) is a minor design smell, not a responsibility of another layer
parsedVerdict.reasoning: PlaceOrderUseCase.execute does the coordinating work expected of an application layer. It checks that each product exists, reserves stock and builds the order through domain operations (catalog.getProduct, catalog.canReserve, catalog.reserve, createOrder), then saves the order through the OrderRepository abstraction. The file has no persistence code, no transport or framework logic, and no presentation concerns. The stock rules themselves sit in the domain: the use case calls canReserve rather than comparing quantities itself. Two borderline points remain. First, the order ID is generated inline from Date.now and Math.random, which would sit better behind an ID-generator port, but it is not a responsibility of a different layer kind. Second, the use case checks every item before reserving any, which is coordination of a multi-step operation.
